}\n  td.n, th.n { white-space: nowrap; font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }\n  caption {\n    caption-side: bottom;\n    padding: 0.65rem 0.95rem 0.8rem;\n    font-size: 0.8rem;\n    line-height: 1.5;\n    color: var(--ink-soft);\n    text-align: left;\n  }\n\n  /* ---- Limitations ---- */\n  .lim h3 .limno {\n    display: inline-block;\n    min-width: 1.7em;\n    color: var(--accent);\n    font-family: var(--serif);\n    font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums;\n  }\n\n  /* ---- Footer ---- */\n  footer {\n    border-top: 1px solid var(--hairline);\n    margin-top: 3.6rem;\n    padding: 2.3rem 0 3.6rem;\n    font-size: 0.92rem;\n    color: var(--ink-soft);\n  }\n  footer .cite { margin: 0 0 0.25rem; max-width: 46rem; }\n  footer .cite .title { font-style: italic; color: var(--ink-mid); }\n  footer .f-links { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1.4rem; margin: 1.1rem 0 0; }\n  footer a { color: var(--accent-deep); }\n  footer .status { max-width: 46rem; margin-top: 1.1rem; }\n\n  /* ---- Tablet / desktop ---- */\n  @media (min-width: 900px) {\n    .cards { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr)); }\n  }\n  @media (min-width: 1024px) {\n    .layout { grid-template-columns: 13.5rem minmax(0, 1fr); column-gap: 3.25rem; }\n    .side-nav {\n      position: sticky;\n      top: 2.4rem;\n      align-self: start;\n      background: none;\n      border-bottom: 0;\n      margin: 0;\n      padding: 0.6rem 0 0;\n      overflow: visible;\n    }\n    .side-nav ul { flex-direction: column; gap: 0.12rem; white-space: normal; padding: 0; border-left: 1px solid var(--hairline); }\n    .side-nav li { margin: 0; }\n    .side-nav a {\n      display: block;\n      padding: 0.42rem 0.95rem;\n      border-bottom: 0;\n      border-left: 2px solid transparent;\n      margin-left: -1px;\n      font-size: 0.86rem;\n      letter-spacing: 0.02em;\n      text-transform: none;\n      font-weight: 570;\n    }\n    .side-nav a[aria-current=\"true\"] { border-bottom: 0; border-left-color: var(--accent); }\n    section { scroll-margin-top: 1.5rem; }\n  }\n\n  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {\n    *, *::before, *::after {\n      animation: none !important;\n      transition: none !important;\n      scroll-behavior: auto !important;\n    }\n  }\n</style>\n</head>\n<body>\n<a class=\"skip-link\" href=\"#main\">Skip to main content</a>\n\n<div class=\"shell\">\n  <div class=\"layout\">\n\n    <nav class=\"side-nav\" id=\"section-nav\" aria-label=\"Page sections\">\n      <ul>\n        <li><a href=\"#overview\">Overview</a></li>\n        <li><a href=\"#contributions\">Contributions</a></li>\n        <li><a href=\"#method\">Method</a></li>\n        <li><a href=\"#results\">Results</a></li>\n        <li><a href=\"#limitations\">Limitations</a></li>\n      </ul>\n    </nav>\n\n    <div class=\"content\">\n\n      <header class=\"hero\" id=\"overview\">\n        <p class=\"kicker\">Pre-registered research design &middot; no model estimated</p>\n        <h1>The Welfare Gate: Pre-Fisc Inequality, Universal Public Services, and Democratic Resilience in Post-1990 Democratizers</h1>\n        <p class=\"lede\">\n          The democratic-erosion literature is split. One camp finds that income inequality is among the strongest\n          predictors of democratic decline in a global sample of uninterrupted democracies [1]. The other, reading the\n          post-1990 wave case by case, finds that economic grievances did not systematically separate backsliders from\n          survivors [2]. This paper argues the dispute is unfalsifiable as both sides run it: the statistical camp\n          tests no conditioning structure, and its flagship treatment, disposable-income inequality, is post-fisc,\n          compressed by exactly the welfare state the gate hypothesis implicates. The registered design corrects both\n          problems. Market-inequality surges, measured pre-fisc, erode the V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index\n          <span class=\"num\">three to five years</span> later only where universal public health and education services\n          built in the first democratic decade are thin. The number that frames the test: the gate holds only if the\n          inequality-by-welfare interaction is significant at <i>p</i>&nbsp;&lt;&nbsp;0.05 in the primary specification\n          and in <span class=\"num\">at least five of the seven</span> robustness cells. No model has been estimated.\n          The estimates do not exist yet; this page is the design.\n        </p>\n        <div class=\"hero-links\">\n          <a class=\"btn primary\" href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-77624d-the-welfare-gate-pre-fisc-inequality@main/paper.pdf\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Read the paper (PDF)</a>\n          <a class=\"btn\" href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-77624d-the-welfare-gate-pre-fisc-inequality\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Code and repository</a>\n        </div>\n      </header>\n\n      <main id=\"main\">\n\n        <section id=\"contributions\" aria-labelledby=\"contributions-h\">\n          <h2 id=\"contributions-h\"><span class=\"idx\">01</span>Contributions</h2>\n          <p class=\"lead\">Four claims, each registered before any estimation.</p>\n          <div class=\"cards\">\n            <div class=\"card\">\n              <h3>Reconciliation on institutional grounds</h3>\n              <p>Neither leading account tests the conditioning structure. This design identifies the condition under\n              which each holds: inequality erodes democracy where welfare institutions are thin, and the coalitional\n              story dominates where they are thick. One interaction test, not two literatures, adjudicates the dispute.</p>\n            </div>\n            <div class=\"card\">\n              <h3>A treatment the institutions cannot compress</h3>\n              <p>Disposable-income inequality is post-fisc, and fiscal systems that compress it are larger where welfare\n              states are larger, so a gate estimated on the disposable Gini cannot separate institutional transmission\n              from arithmetic filtering. The treatment moves pre-fisc, to the WID pre-tax top-10 percent income share,\n              and the market-minus-disposable Gini gap is measured directly, turning the entanglement into a test of\n              the stabilization mechanism.</p>\n            </div>\n            <div class=\"card\">\n              <h3>The democratic dividend, conditioned</h3>\n              <p>Democratization raises tax revenues and schooling but shows no robust average effect on inequality.\n              The design states the dividend on top-income shares over a fixed post-transition window, years 0 to 7,\n              and links its size to regime resilience in 2010&ndash;2022: the inequality-reduction leg materializes\n              only in high-welfare-legacy countries.</p>\n            </div>\n            <div class=\"card\">\n              <h3>Identification and power fixed before the results</h3>\n              <p>The gate is identified off deviations from welfare-specific trends, with estimators built for\n              differential treatment timing, a fixed roster with a documented coverage matrix, exogeneity probes, and\n              a simulation-based minimum-detectable-effect analysis. The confirmation criteria are calibrated to the\n              power the sample can actually deliver.</p>\n            </div>\n          </div>\n        </section>\n\n        <section id=\"method\" aria-labelledby=\"method-h\">\n          <h2 id=\"method-h\"><span class=\"idx\">02</span>Method</h2>\n\n          <h3>The dispute neither side can resolve</h3>\n          <p>Rau and Stokes estimate a main effect: in a sample of democracies uninterrupted over 1995&ndash;2020, the\n          Gini coefficient is among the strongest predictors of erosion onset, with <span class=\"num\">23 spells of\n          backsliding in 22 countries</span>. Haggard and Kaufman compare backsliders with survivors and conclude that\n          economic grievances did not do the separating; polarization and elite coalitional choices did. The\n          statistical account contains no welfare variables, so it cannot see whether its inequality coefficient is\n          carried by thin-welfare democracies. The case-based account never formalizes the interaction a conditional\n          claim requires. Both miss the same object, and the field's flagship treatment is entangled with it:\n          disposable income is post-fisc, and the fiscal systems that compress it are the welfare states this\n          hypothesis implicates.</p>\n\n          <h3>What goes in</h3>\n          <ul class=\"blocks\">\n            <li><strong>Sample.</strong> Post-1990 democratizers with transitions beginning 1989&ndash;1998, an\n            expected roster of <span class=\"num\">25 to 35 countries</span> over a panel running 1985&ndash;2023. The\n            cohort cap makes pre-determination possible: every retained case's first democratic decade ends before the\n            2008 crisis and before the 2010&ndash;2022 resilience window. Transition is dated from the V-Dem Regimes\n            of the World series and cross-checked against Boix&ndash;Miller&ndash;Rosato; the roster is fixed\n            deterministically, and no case is added or dropped after estimation begins.</li>\n            <li><strong>Treatment.</strong> The primary treatment is the World Inequality Database pre-tax\n            national-income top-10 percent income share, the measure type Rau and Stokes use at the top end of\n            their own analysis. It is lagged three years in the main specification, with distributed lags tracing\n            years one through six, implementing the three-to-five-year transmission window. The market-income Gini is\n            the secondary treatment; the disposable Gini, where the entanglement lives, enters only to construct the\n            gap.</li>\n            <li><strong>Gate.</strong> The welfare variable <i>W</i> is the sum of government health expenditure and\n            government education expenditure, both as a share of GDP, averaged over the earliest available three-year\n            window within years 0 to 8 after transition and held time-invariant. It is deliberately non-cash: health\n            and education are what the broad middle class uses, what is automatic in delivery, and what an eroding\n            executive must capture. Pensions and targeted cash are excluded by construction, and they become the\n            placebo moderators of H5.</li>\n            <li><strong>Outcome.</strong> The V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index, 0 to 1, in levels and in five-year\n            differences. A continuous index is essential: the hypothesis concerns graded erosion inside formally\n            democratic regimes. Erosion onset is coded as the first year of a sustained three-year decline of at\n            least <span class=\"num\">0.03</span>.</li>\n          </ul>\n\n          <h3>The gate and its two paths</h3>\n          <p>A market shock reaches liberal-democratic quality through two terms, and the design measures them\n          separately. The first is arithmetic: the market-minus-disposable Gini gap absorbs part of any shock before\n          the distribution reaches citizens, and this works even if no citizen changes behavior. The second is\n          behavioral: the residue of the shock that does reach citizens, gated by constituency formation, by which a\n          middle class that uses public services holds a material stake in the institutions erosion would capture,\n          and by credible pre-commitment, by which universal automatic programs block the populist-promise\n          equilibrium.</p>\n          <div class=\"eq\" aria-hidden=\"true\">\n            <span class=\"term\">d&#8201;LibDem / d&#8201;m = [ &part;LibDem/&part;d &middot; (1 &minus; &phi;(W)) ]\n            <span class=\"lbl\">fiscal filtering</span></span>\n            <span class=\"op\">+</span>\n            <span class=\"term\">[ &part;LibDem/&part;m | d&#772; ]\n            <span class=\"lbl\">behavioral transmission</span></span>\n          </div>\n          <p>A design that treats disposable inequality as the treatment and welfare as the moderator conflates the\n          two terms. This design treats the pre-fisc shock as the treatment and enters the gap directly, as a\n          covariate and as a moderator. If gap control drives the interaction to zero, automatic stabilization is the\n          entire mechanism. If the interaction survives, a behavioral residue exists, and Designs 5 and 6 exist to\n          attribute it.</p>\n\n          <h3>Estimating the gate</h3>\n          <p>The core specification, Design 1, is a two-way fixed-effects regression with welfare-specific trends:</p>\n          <div class=\"eq\" aria-hidden=\"true\">\n            LibDem<sub>it</sub> = &alpha;<sub>i</sub> + &delta;<sub>t</sub> + &beta;<sub>1</sub>&#8201;m<sub>i,t&minus;3</sub>\n            + &beta;<sub>2</sub>(m<sub>i,t&minus;3</sub> &times; W<sub>i</sub>)\n            + &gamma;<sub>1</sub>W<sub>i</sub>t + &gamma;<sub>2</sub>W<sub>i</sub>t<sup>2</sup>\n            + X&prime;<sub>it</sub>&theta; + &epsilon;<sub>it</sub>\n          </div>\n          <p>The interaction coefficient &beta;<sub>2</sub> is the gate. Hypothesis H1 is &beta;<sub>2</sub> &gt; 0,\n          with the marginal effect near zero or positive in the high-welfare arm and strongly negative in the\n          thin-welfare arm, reported at the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentiles of the welfare distribution.\n          The welfare-specific trends are the identification change this registration makes: any factor correlated\n          with welfare strength and with democratic trajectories, EU accession, fiscal capacity, geopolitical\n          alignment, is absorbed in the trend terms, and the gate is identified off deviations from welfare-specific\n          trends. Because two-way fixed effects with differential timing can be biased under heterogeneous effects,\n          the interacted specification is also estimated on five-year differences of the outcome, with\n          Goodman&ndash;Bacon decompositions, Callaway&ndash;Sant'Anna and Sun&ndash;Abraham estimators in the event\n          studies, and wild cluster bootstrap inference for the interaction test.</p>\n\n          <h3>The six designs</h3>\n          <ol class=\"designs\">\n            <li><strong>Design 1, the gate test.</strong> The two-way fixed-effects specification with welfare-specific\n            trends, plus the gap-controlled variant whose reading is fixed in advance.</li>\n            <li><strong>Design 2, the adjudication.</strong> The inequality main effect with and without the\n            interaction, on the full democracy sample and on the young-democracy sample. A weak main effect with a\n            strong interaction reconciles the two accounts. A surviving unconditional effect favors the materialist\n            account; a null everywhere favors the coalitional account.</li>\n            <li><strong>Design 3, sequencing.</strong> Erosion-onset event studies estimated separately in the\n            high-welfare and thin-welfare arms, with pre-trend tests. The lead-lag structure is the primary defense\n            against reverse causality: services must fall before the index in the thin-welfare arm, and not at all in\n            the high-welfare arm.</li>\n            <li><strong>Design 4, the dividend.</strong> A democratization event study aligned at transition, tracing\n            the top-10 percent share, services and education over two decades by welfare legacy. The dividend window\n            is fixed at years 0 to 7, so it precedes the 2008 crisis and the 2010&ndash;2022 resilience window for\n            every retained case.</li>\n            <li><strong>Design 5, mechanisms.</strong> Four arms: gap control for stabilization; composition and\n            usage controls for constituency formation; the automaticity index for pre-commitment; and a\n            proximate-channel report on polarization and educated-youth unemployment.</li>\n            <li><strong>Design 6, robustness.</strong> Seven pre-committed cells, every one reported including the\n            failures: alternative treatments, alternative welfare measures, population weights, commodity-boom\n            exclusion, within-Eastern-Europe estimates and the early-erosion exclusion, wild cluster bootstrap\n            inference, and the placebo moderators.</li>\n          </ol>\n\n          <h3>Why the design is shaped this way</h3>\n          <p>Everything hangs on one logical move: the pre-determined must precede the outcome it explains. Welfare\n          institutions built in the first democratic decade, before crises arrive, gate the inequality-erosion link;\n          welfare generosity purchased later by incumbents is not a substitute, it is part of the erosion playbook.\n          Five exogeneity probes confront the threat that the first democratic decade itself selects welfare depth:\n          balancing regressions of <i>W</i> on first-decade inequality changes and fiscal collapse; legacy-instrument\n          2SLS using communist-era schooling enrollment and colonial-era public-service coverage; the\n          within-Eastern-Europe estimate, which holds the communist legacy constant; the placebo moderator, which\n          predicts that a pension-heavy total-spending measure does not gate; and the early-erosion exclusion, which\n          removes cases for which <i>W</i> is post-treatment by construction.</p>\n          <p>The power analysis is calibrated to the same honesty. Minimum detectable effects are simulated on the\n          realized panel at <span class=\"num\">80 percent power</span>, under outcome serial correlation of 0.7, 0.8\n          and 0.9 and effective N of 25, 30 and 35. The study is powered to detect a large conditional effect, which\n          is what the theory predicts. A weak gate will go undetected, and the results paper will say so rather than\n          claim a null.</p>\n\n          <h3>The five hypotheses</h3>\n          <dl class=\"hyps\">\n            <dt><span class=\"hno\">H1</span> &middot; The gate</dt>\n            <dd>The within-country effect of a lagged market-inequality increase on the Liberal Democracy Index is\n            negative and large in thin-welfare countries and near zero or positive in strong-welfare countries; the\n            interaction is positive and significant under welfare-specific trend controls.</dd>\n            <dt><span class=\"hno\">H2</span> &middot; Sequencing</dt>\n            <dd>Market-inequality surges and public-services retrenchment lead liberal-democracy declines by three to\n            five years in thin-welfare countries, with no anticipatory service decline before erosion onset in\n            high-welfare countries.</dd>\n            <dt><span class=\"hno\">H3</span> &middot; The welfare-dependent dividend</dt>\n            <dd>Democratization reduces the top-10 percent income share in the first post-transition years only in\n            high-welfare-legacy countries, and the size of that first-decade decline predicts 2010&ndash;2022\n            resilience.</dd>\n            <dt><span class=\"hno\">H4</span> &middot; Mechanisms</dt>\n            <dd>At least one discriminating result: gap control kills the interaction (stabilization); composition and\n            usage controls attenuate it (constituency formation); automatic programs gate and discretionary transfers\n            do not (pre-commitment); or the interaction runs through polarization and tightens where education\n            expands without absorption.</dd>\n            <dt><span class=\"hno\">H5</span> &middot; The universalism contrast</dt>\n            <dd>Public health and education services gate; total social spending, pension-heavy and\n            transfer-dominated, and late-bought targeted or chauvinist transfers are placebo moderators that do not\n            gate.</dd>\n          </dl>\n        </section>\n\n        <section id=\"results\" aria-labelledby=\"results-h\">\n          <h2 id=\"results-h\"><span class=\"idx\">03</span>Results</h2>\n          <p class=\"lead\">The paper reports no estimates; none exist yet. What follows are the numbers the design is\n          built around, each as it appears in the paper: the calibration that frames the dispute, the trajectories\n          the design must explain, and the decision rules fixed before estimation.</p>\n\n          <h3>The calibration that frames the dispute</h3>\n          <p>Rau and Stokes calibrate their leading predictor against predicted annual erosion risk. Their sample:\n          23 spells of backsliding in 22 countries over 1995&ndash;2020, nine years on average, with main analyses\n          covering <span class=\"num\">92 countries</span>.</p>\n          <div class=\"table-wrap\">\n            <table>\n              <caption>Predicted annual risk of erosion onset by country, from Rau and Stokes 2025, as reported in\n              Section 2.1 of the paper.</caption>\n              <thead>\n                <tr>\n                  <th scope=\"col\">Country</th>\n                  <th scope=\"col\">Measured on</th>\n                  <th scope=\"col\" class=\"n\">Predicted annual risk</th>\n                  <th scope=\"col\">Compared with</th>\n                </tr>\n              </thead>\n              <tbody>\n                <tr>\n                  <td>Sweden</td>\n                  <td>Gini of 26.4 in 2017</td>\n                  <td class=\"n\">4 percent</td>\n                  <td>more equal than 87 percent of democracies</td>\n                </tr>\n                <tr>\n                  <td>United States</td>\n                  <td>Gini of 38.4</td>\n                  <td class=\"n\">8.4 percent</td>\n                  <td>exceeds 60 percent of democracies</td>\n                </tr>\n                <tr>\n                  <td>South Africa</td>\n                  <td>most unequal democracy in the sample</td>\n                  <td class=\"n\">31 percent</td>\n                  <td>&mdash;</td>\n                </tr>\n              </tbody>\n            </table>\n          </div>\n          <p>The democratic-dividend literature supplies the second calibration: democratization raises the tax-to-GDP\n          ratio by about <span class=\"num\">16 percent</span> in the long run in the preferred specification, with no\n          robust average effect on inequality. The null is the field fact the gate explains.</p>\n\n          <h3>The trajectories the design must explain</h3>\n          <p>Among the eleven cases with continuous data, liberal-democratic quality diverged sharply after 2010.\n          The same wave produced both the sharpest erosion and the most stable resilience in the same region. EU accession was itself a welfare-building force, so the\n          gate and the accession channel are partially entangled by construction.</p>\n          <h3><span class=\"limno\">4.</span>Measurement of the outcome and the treatment</h3>\n          <p>The Liberal Democracy Index is expert-coded, and its inter-temporal comparability is contested. Gini\n          comparability is limited by differing underlying surveys and income concepts; PIP and WID harmonization\n          does not remove the issue. The three-year sustained-decline coding rule, alternative\n          onset codings, and the requirement that the sequencing pattern differ across welfare arms address it, and a\n          pure measurement artifact would not produce that difference.</p>\n          <h3><span class=\"limno\">5.</span>The placebo subsample problem</h3>\n          <p>The sharpest contrast, H5, requires a full-sample placebo. border-left-color: var(--accent); }\n    section { scroll-margin-top: 1.5rem; }\n  }\n\n  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {\n    *, *::before, *::after {\n      animation: none !important;\n      transition: none !important;\n      scroll-behavior: auto !important;\n    }\n  }\n</style>\n</head>\n<body>\n<a class=\"skip-link\" href=\"#main\">Skip to main content</a>\n\n<div class=\"shell\">\n  <div class=\"layout\">\n\n    <nav class=\"side-nav\" id=\"section-nav\" aria-label=\"Page sections\">\n      <ul>\n        <li><a href=\"#overview\">Overview</a></li>\n        <li><a href=\"#contributions\">Contributions</a></li>\n        <li><a href=\"#method\">Method</a></li>\n        <li><a href=\"#results\">Results</a></li>\n        <li><a href=\"#limitations\">Limitations</a></li>\n      </ul>\n    </nav>\n\n    <div class=\"content\">\n\n      <header class=\"hero\" id=\"overview\">\n        <p class=\"kicker\">Pre-registered research design &middot; no model estimated</p>\n        <h1>The Welfare Gate: Pre-Fisc Inequality, Universal Public Services, and Democratic Resilience in Post-1990 Democratizers</h1>\n        <p class=\"lede\">\n          The democratic-erosion literature is split. One camp finds that income inequality is among the strongest\n          predictors of democratic decline in a global sample of uninterrupted democracies [1]. The other, reading the\n          post-1990 wave case by case, finds that economic grievances did not systematically separate backsliders from\n          survivors [2]. This paper argues the dispute is unfalsifiable as both sides run it: the statistical camp\n          tests no conditioning structure, and its flagship treatment, disposable-income inequality, is post-fisc,\n          compressed by exactly the welfare state the gate hypothesis implicates. The registered design corrects both\n          problems. Market-inequality surges, measured pre-fisc, erode the V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index\n          <span class=\"num\">three to five years</span> later only where universal public health and education services\n          built in the first democratic decade are thin. The number that frames the test: the gate holds only if the\n          inequality-by-welfare interaction is significant at <i>p</i>&nbsp;&lt;&nbsp;0.05 in the primary specification\n          and in <span class=\"num\">at least five of the seven</span> robustness cells. No model has been estimated.\n          The estimates do not exist yet; this page is the design.\n        </p>\n        <div class=\"hero-links\">\n          <a class=\"btn primary\" href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-77624d-the-welfare-gate-pre-fisc-inequality@main/paper.pdf\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Read the paper (PDF)</a>\n          <a class=\"btn\" href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-77624d-the-welfare-gate-pre-fisc-inequality\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Code and repository</a>\n        </div>\n      </header>\n\n      <main id=\"main\">\n\n        <section id=\"contributions\" aria-labelledby=\"contributions-h\">\n          <h2 id=\"contributions-h\"><span class=\"idx\">01</span>Contributions</h2>\n          <p class=\"lead\">Four claims, each registered before any estimation.</p>\n          <div class=\"cards\">\n            <div class=\"card\">\n              <h3>Reconciliation on institutional grounds</h3>\n              <p>Neither leading account tests the conditioning structure. This design identifies the condition under\n              which each holds: inequality erodes democracy where welfare institutions are thin, and the coalitional\n              story dominates where they are thick. One interaction test, not two literatures, adjudicates the dispute.</p>\n            </div>\n            <div class=\"card\">\n              <h3>A treatment the institutions cannot compress</h3>\n              <p>Disposable-income inequality is post-fisc, and fiscal systems that compress it are larger where welfare\n              states are larger, so a gate estimated on the disposable Gini cannot separate institutional transmission\n              from arithmetic filtering. The treatment moves pre-fisc, to the WID pre-tax top-10 percent income share,\n              and the market-minus-disposable Gini gap is measured directly, turning the entanglement into a test of\n              the stabilization mechanism.</p>\n            </div>\n            <div class=\"card\">\n              <h3>The democratic dividend, conditioned</h3>\n              <p>Democratization raises tax revenues and schooling but shows no robust average effect on inequality.\n              The design states the dividend on top-income shares over a fixed post-transition window, years 0 to 7,\n              and links its size to regime resilience in 2010&ndash;2022: the inequality-reduction leg materializes\n              only in high-welfare-legacy countries.</p>\n            </div>\n            <div class=\"card\">\n              <h3>Identification and power fixed before the results</h3>\n              <p>The gate is identified off deviations from welfare-specific trends, with estimators built for\n              differential treatment timing, a fixed roster with a documented coverage matrix, exogeneity probes, and\n              a simulation-based minimum-detectable-effect analysis. The confirmation criteria are calibrated to the\n              power the sample can actually deliver.</p>\n            </div>\n          </div>\n        </section>\n\n        <section id=\"method\" aria-labelledby=\"method-h\">\n          <h2 id=\"method-h\"><span class=\"idx\">02</span>Method</h2>\n\n          <h3>The dispute neither side can resolve</h3>\n          <p>Rau and Stokes estimate a main effect: in a sample of democracies uninterrupted over 1995&ndash;2020, the\n          Gini coefficient is among the strongest predictors of erosion onset, with <span class=\"num\">23 spells of\n          backsliding in 22 countries</span>. Haggard and Kaufman compare backsliders with survivors and conclude that\n          economic grievances did not do the separating; polarization and elite coalitional choices did. The\n          statistical account contains no welfare variables, so it cannot see whether its inequality coefficient is\n          carried by thin-welfare democracies. The case-based account never formalizes the interaction a conditional\n          claim requires. Both miss the same object, and the field's flagship treatment is entangled with it:\n          disposable income is post-fisc, and the fiscal systems that compress it are the welfare states this\n          hypothesis implicates.</p>\n\n          <h3>What goes in</h3>\n          <ul class=\"blocks\">\n            <li><strong>Sample.</strong> Post-1990 democratizers with transitions beginning 1989&ndash;1998, an\n            expected roster of <span class=\"num\">25 to 35 countries</span> over a panel running 1985&ndash;2023. The\n            cohort cap makes pre-determination possible: every retained case's first democratic decade ends before the\n            2008 crisis and before the 2010&ndash;2022 resilience window. Transition is dated from the V-Dem Regimes\n            of the World series and cross-checked against Boix&ndash;Miller&ndash;Rosato; the roster is fixed\n            deterministically, and no case is added or dropped after estimation begins.</li>\n            <li><strong>Treatment.</strong> The primary treatment is the World Inequality Database pre-tax\n            national-income top-10 percent income share, the measure type Rau and Stokes use at the top end of\n            their own analysis. It is lagged three years in the main specification, with distributed lags tracing\n            years one through six, implementing the three-to-five-year transmission window. The market-income Gini is\n            the secondary treatment; the disposable Gini, where the entanglement lives, enters only to construct the\n            gap.</li>\n            <li><strong>Gate.</strong> The welfare variable <i>W</i> is the sum of government health expenditure and\n            government education expenditure, both as a share of GDP, averaged over the earliest available three-year\n            window within years 0 to 8 after transition and held time-invariant. It is deliberately non-cash: health\n            and education are what the broad middle class uses, what is automatic in delivery, and what an eroding\n            executive must capture. Pensions and targeted cash are excluded by construction, and they become the\n            placebo moderators of H5.</li>\n            <li><strong>Outcome.</strong> The V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index, 0 to 1, in levels and in five-year\n            differences. A continuous index is essential: the hypothesis concerns graded erosion inside formally\n            democratic regimes. Erosion onset is coded as the first year of a sustained three-year decline of at\n            least <span class=\"num\">0.03</span>.</li>\n          </ul>\n\n          <h3>The gate and its two paths</h3>\n          <p>A market shock reaches liberal-democratic quality through two terms, and the design measures them\n          separately. The first is arithmetic: the market-minus-disposable Gini gap absorbs part of any shock before\n          the distribution reaches citizens, and this works even if no citizen changes behavior. The second is\n          behavioral: the residue of the shock that does reach citizens, gated by constituency formation, by which a\n          middle class that uses public services holds a material stake in the institutions erosion would capture,\n          and by credible pre-commitment, by which universal automatic programs block the populist-promise\n          equilibrium.</p>\n          <div class=\"eq\" aria-hidden=\"true\">\n            <span class=\"term\">d&#8201;LibDem / d&#8201;m = [ &part;LibDem/&part;d &middot; (1 &minus; &phi;(W)) ]\n            <span class=\"lbl\">fiscal filtering</span></span>\n            <span class=\"op\">+</span>\n            <span class=\"term\">[ &part;LibDem/&part;m | d&#772; ]\n            <span class=\"lbl\">behavioral transmission</span></span>\n          </div>\n          <p>A design that treats disposable inequality as the treatment and welfare as the moderator conflates the\n          two terms. This design treats the pre-fisc shock as the treatment and enters the gap directly, as a\n          covariate and as a moderator. If gap control drives the interaction to zero, automatic stabilization is the\n          entire mechanism. If the interaction survives, a behavioral residue exists, and Designs 5 and 6 exist to\n          attribute it.</p>\n\n          <h3>Estimating the gate</h3>\n          <p>The core specification, Design 1, is a two-way fixed-effects regression with welfare-specific trends:</p>\n          <div class=\"eq\" aria-hidden=\"true\">\n            LibDem<sub>it</sub> = &alpha;<sub>i</sub> + &delta;<sub>t</sub> + &beta;<sub>1</sub>&#8201;m<sub>i,t&minus;3</sub>\n            + &beta;<sub>2</sub>(m<sub>i,t&minus;3</sub> &times; W<sub>i</sub>)\n            + &gamma;<sub>1</sub>W<sub>i</sub>t + &gamma;<sub>2</sub>W<sub>i</sub>t<sup>2</sup>\n            + X&prime;<sub>it</sub>&theta; + &epsilon;<sub>it</sub>\n          </div>\n          <p>The interaction coefficient &beta;<sub>2</sub> is the gate. Hypothesis H1 is &beta;<sub>2</sub> &gt; 0,\n          with the marginal effect near zero or positive in the high-welfare arm and strongly negative in the\n          thin-welfare arm, reported at the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentiles of the welfare distribution.\n          The welfare-specific trends are the identification change this registration makes: any factor correlated\n          with welfare strength and with democratic trajectories, EU accession, fiscal capacity, geopolitical\n          alignment, is absorbed in the trend terms, and the gate is identified off deviations from welfare-specific\n          trends. Because two-way fixed effects with differential timing can be biased under heterogeneous effects,\n          the interacted specification is also estimated on five-year differences of the outcome, with\n          Goodman&ndash;Bacon decompositions, Callaway&ndash;Sant'Anna and Sun&ndash;Abraham estimators in the event\n          studies, and wild cluster bootstrap inference for the interaction test.</p>\n\n          <h3>The six designs</h3>\n          <ol class=\"designs\">\n            <li><strong>Design 1, the gate test.</strong> The two-way fixed-effects specification with welfare-specific\n            trends, plus the gap-controlled variant whose reading is fixed in advance.</li>\n            <li><strong>Design 2, the adjudication.</strong> The inequality main effect with and without the\n            interaction, on the full democracy sample and on the young-democracy sample. A weak main effect with a\n            strong interaction reconciles the two accounts. A surviving unconditional effect favors the materialist\n            account; a null everywhere favors the coalitional account.</li>\n            <li><strong>Design 3, sequencing.</strong> Erosion-onset event studies estimated separately in the\n            high-welfare and thin-welfare arms, with pre-trend tests. The lead-lag structure is the primary defense\n            against reverse causality: services must fall before the index in the thin-welfare arm, and not at all in\n            the high-welfare arm.</li>\n            <li><strong>Design 4, the dividend.</strong> A democratization event study aligned at transition, tracing\n            the top-10 percent share, services and education over two decades by welfare legacy. The dividend window\n            is fixed at years 0 to 7, so it precedes the 2008 crisis and the 2010&ndash;2022 resilience window for\n            every retained case.</li>\n            <li><strong>Design 5, mechanisms.</strong> Four arms: gap control for stabilization; composition and\n            usage controls for constituency formation; the automaticity index for pre-commitment; and a\n            proximate-channel report on polarization and educated-youth unemployment.</li>\n            <li><strong>Design 6, robustness.</strong> Seven pre-committed cells, every one reported including the\n            failures: alternative treatments, alternative welfare measures, population weights, commodity-boom\n            exclusion, within-Eastern-Europe estimates and the early-erosion exclusion, wild cluster bootstrap\n            inference, and the placebo moderators.</li>\n          </ol>\n\n          <h3>Why the design is shaped this way</h3>\n          <p>Everything hangs on one logical move: the pre-determined must precede the outcome it explains. Welfare\n          institutions built in the first democratic decade, before crises arrive, gate the inequality-erosion link;\n          welfare generosity purchased later by incumbents is not a substitute, it is part of the erosion playbook.\n          Five exogeneity probes confront the threat that the first democratic decade itself selects welfare depth:\n          balancing regressions of <i>W</i> on first-decade inequality changes and fiscal collapse; legacy-instrument\n          2SLS using communist-era schooling enrollment and colonial-era public-service coverage; the\n          within-Eastern-Europe estimate, which holds the communist legacy constant; the placebo moderator, which\n          predicts that a pension-heavy total-spending measure does not gate; and the early-erosion exclusion, which\n          removes cases for which <i>W</i> is post-treatment by construction.</p>\n          <p>The power analysis is calibrated to the same honesty. Minimum detectable effects are simulated on the\n          realized panel at <span class=\"num\">80 percent power</span>, under outcome serial correlation of 0.7, 0.8\n          and 0.9 and effective N of 25, 30 and 35. The study is powered to detect a large conditional effect, which\n          is what the theory predicts. A weak gate will go undetected, and the results paper will say so rather than\n          claim a null.</p>\n\n          <h3>The five hypotheses</h3>\n          <dl class=\"hyps\">\n            <dt><span class=\"hno\">H1</span> &middot; The gate</dt>\n            <dd>The within-country effect of a lagged market-inequality increase on the Liberal Democracy Index is\n            negative and large in thin-welfare countries and near zero or positive in strong-welfare countries; the\n            interaction is positive and significant under welfare-specific trend controls.</dd>\n            <dt><span class=\"hno\">H2</span> &middot; Sequencing</dt>\n            <dd>Market-inequality surges and public-services retrenchment lead liberal-democracy declines by three to\n            five years in thin-welfare countries, with no anticipatory service decline before erosion onset in\n            high-welfare countries.</dd>\n            <dt><span class=\"hno\">H3</span> &middot; The welfare-dependent dividend</dt>\n            <dd>Democratization reduces the top-10 percent income share in the first post-transition years only in\n            high-welfare-legacy countries, and the size of that first-decade decline predicts 2010&ndash;2022\n            resilience.</dd>\n            <dt><span class=\"hno\">H4</span> &middot; Mechanisms</dt>\n            <dd>At least one discriminating result: gap control kills the interaction (stabilization); composition and\n            usage controls attenuate it (constituency formation); automatic programs gate and discretionary transfers\n            do not (pre-commitment); or the interaction runs through polarization and tightens where education\n            expands without absorption.</dd>\n            <dt><span class=\"hno\">H5</span> &middot; The universalism contrast</dt>\n            <dd>Public health and education services gate; total social spending, pension-heavy and\n            transfer-dominated, and late-bought targeted or chauvinist transfers are placebo moderators that do not\n            gate.</dd>\n          </dl>\n        </section>\n\n        <section id=\"results\" aria-labelledby=\"results-h\">\n          <h2 id=\"results-h\"><span class=\"idx\">03</span>Results</h2>\n          <p class=\"lead\">The paper reports no estimates; none exist yet. What follows are the numbers the design is\n          built around, each as it appears in the paper: the calibration that frames the dispute, the trajectories\n          the design must explain, and the decision rules fixed before estimation.</p>\n\n          <h3>The calibration that frames the dispute</h3>\n          <p>Rau and Stokes calibrate their leading predictor against predicted annual erosion risk. Their sample:\n          23 spells of backsliding in 22 countries over 1995&ndash;2020, nine years on average, with main analyses\n          covering <span class=\"num\">92 countries</span>.</p>\n          <div class=\"table-wrap\">\n            <table>\n              <caption>Predicted annual risk of erosion onset by country, from Rau and Stokes 2025, as reported in\n              Section 2.1 of the paper.</caption>\n              <thead>\n                <tr>\n                  <th scope=\"col\">Country</th>\n                  <th scope=\"col\">Measured on</th>\n                  <th scope=\"col\" class=\"n\">Predicted annual risk</th>\n                  <th scope=\"col\">Compared with</th>\n                </tr>\n              </thead>\n              <tbody>\n                <tr>\n                  <td>Sweden</td>\n                  <td>Gini of 26.4 in 2017</td>\n                  <td class=\"n\">4 percent</td>\n                  <td>more equal than 87 percent of democracies</td>\n                </tr>\n                <tr>\n                  <td>United States</td>\n                  <td>Gini of 38.4</td>\n                  <td class=\"n\">8.4 percent</td>\n                  <td>exceeds 60 percent of democracies</td>\n                </tr>\n                <tr>\n                  <td>South Africa</td>\n                  <td>most unequal democracy in the sample</td>\n                  <td class=\"n\">31 percent</td>\n                  <td>&mdash;</td>\n                </tr>\n              </tbody>\n            </table>\n          </div>\n          <p>The democratic-dividend literature supplies the second calibration: democratization raises the tax-to-GDP\n          ratio by about <span class=\"num\">16 percent</span> in the long run in the preferred specification, with no\n          robust average effect on inequality. The null is the field fact the gate explains.</p>\n\n          <h3>The trajectories the design must explain</h3>\n          <p>Among the eleven cases with continuous data, liberal-democratic quality diverged sharply after 2010.\n          The same wave produced both the sharpest erosion and the most stable resilience in the same region. Welfare\n          sums are the development-phase measure of <i>W</i>, health plus education spending as a share of GDP.</p>\n          <div class=\"table-wrap\">\n            <table>\n              <caption>Liberal Democracy Index (0&ndash;1) and welfare sums by country, from Section 4.7 of the\n              paper. Values from the development phase, to be re-verified at every series URL in the coverage audit.</caption>\n              <thead>\n                <tr>\n                  <th scope=\"col\">Country</th>\n                  <th scope=\"col\">Liberal Democracy Index</th>\n                  <th scope=\"col\" class=\"n\">Welfare sum, % of GDP</th>\n                </tr>\n              </thead>\n              <tbody>\n                <tr><td>Hungary</td><td>0.754 in 2005 &rarr; 0.335 in 2022</td><td class=\"n\">9.6</td></tr>\n                <tr><td>Poland</td><td>0.827 in 2010 &rarr; 0.417 in 2022</td><td class=\"n\">8.9</td></tr>\n                <tr><td>Estonia</td><td>0.811 &rarr; 0.853, 2010&ndash;2022</td><td class=\"n\">9.5</td></tr>\n                <tr><td>Slovakia</td><td>held its 2005 level</td><td class=\"n\">9.0</td></tr>\n                <tr><td>Latvia</td><td>held its 2005 level</td><td class=\"n\">8.4</td></tr>\n                <tr><td>Lithuania</td><td>held its 2005 level</td><td class=\"n\">10.3</td></tr>\n                <tr><td>Chile</td><td>consolidated after 2000, declined mildly after 2015</td><td class=\"n\">7.5</td></tr>\n                <tr><td>South Korea</td><td>fell mid-decade, recovered, ended 2022 at 0.718</td><td class=\"n\">5.1</td></tr>\n                <tr><td>South Africa</td><td>0.666 in 2010 &rarr; 0.610 in 2022</td><td class=\"n\">7.2</td></tr>\n                <tr><td>Bulgaria, Romania</td><td>fluctuated in an intermediate band; no usable WHO health series in the early window on OWID</td><td class=\"n\">&mdash;</td></tr>\n              </tbody>\n            </table>\n          </div>\n          <p>The inequality levels do not line up with the erosion outcomes. Hungary's disposable Gini ran between\n          0.27 and 0.35 over 2005&ndash;2016, with a trough of 0.270 in 2009; Poland's fell from 0.38 in 2004 to 0.31\n          in 2016. The resilient countries were not the most equal: Estonia's Gini held between 0.31 and 0.35,\n          Latvia's between 0.34 and 0.39. The level correlation is weak in exactly the way Haggard and Kaufman\n          describe, which is why the theory is stated in shocks rather than levels: the gate conditions the\n          transmission of inequality increases, not the standing level of inequality.</p>\n          <p>South Africa is the sharpest case: the cohort's highest inequality, a Gini near 0.65 at its 2005 peak\n          and still 0.61 in 2010, with only modest liberal-democratic decline, from 0.666 in 2010 to 0.610 in 2022.\n          The paper reads the pattern as delayed or partial transmission, and the Design 3 timing tests are what\n          distinguish that reading from a materialist one.</p>\n\n          <h3>Decision rules fixed ex ante</h3>\n          <div class=\"table-wrap\">\n            <table>\n              <caption>Rules from Sections 5 and 6 of the paper. Every rule is fixed and deposited in a timestamped\n              OSF registry before estimation; no specification is added or dropped after.</caption>\n              <thead>\n                <tr>\n                  <th scope=\"col\">Rule</th>\n                  <th scope=\"col\">Committed value</th>\n                </tr>\n              </thead>\n              <tbody>\n                <tr><td>Primary specification</td><td>Design 1 with the pre-fisc treatment, the earliest-window <i>W</i>, and welfare-specific trends</td></tr>\n                <tr><td>Significance rule</td><td>Interaction significant at <i>p</i> &lt; 0.05, with the marginal effect negative and excluding zero at the 10th and 25th percentiles of <i>W</i> and not significantly negative at the 90th percentile</td></tr>\n                <tr><td>Robustness rule</td><td>Pattern confirmed in the primary specification and in at least five of the seven robustness cells; failures reported and interpreted</td></tr>\n                <tr><td>Transmission window</td><td>Surges lead declines by three to five years; treatment lagged three years, distributed lags tracing years one through six</td></tr>\n                <tr><td>Power</td><td>Simulation-based MDES at 80 percent power, outcome serial correlation 0.7, 0.8 and 0.9, effective N 25, 30 and 35</td></tr>\n                <tr><td>Cohort and roster</td><td>Transitions beginning 1989&ndash;1998; expected roster 25 to 35 countries; panel 1985&ndash;2023</td></tr>\n                <tr><td>Dividend window</td><td>Years 0 to 7 after transition; the decline's size predicts the 2010&ndash;2022 change in the Liberal Democracy Index</td></tr>\n                <tr><td>Welfare windows</td><td>Primary: earliest available three-year window within years 0 to 8; sensitivity pairs T+3 to T+7 and T+8 to T+12</td></tr>\n                <tr><td>Erosion onset coding</td><td>First year of a sustained three-year decline of at least 0.03 in the index</td></tr>\n                <tr><td>Early-erosion exclusion</td><td>Cases with onset within the first twelve years are excluded pre-committed under Design 6(e)</td></tr>\n              </tbody>\n            </table>\n          </div>\n        </section>\n\n        <section id=\"limitations\" class=\"lim\" aria-labelledby=\"limitations-h\">\n          <h2 id=\"limitations-h\"><span class=\"idx\">04</span>Limitations</h2>\n          <p class=\"lead\">Five limitations are intrinsic to the design, and the paper states them as such rather than\n          as future work (Section 8).</p>\n          <h3><span class=\"limno\">1.</span>Small N and statistical power</h3>\n          <p>The treated sample is 25 to 35 countries, and the interaction is a difference-in-differences of a\n          difference-in-differences. Power for interaction tests is low in samples of this size, and the clustered\n          standard errors rest on a modest number of clusters. The pre-committed MDES analysis defines what the\n          design can detect before estimation; the study will not detect a weak gate, and the results paper will say\n          so if the confidence intervals cannot exclude one.</p>\n          <h3><span class=\"limno\">2.</span>The welfare measure is a proxy</h3>\n          <p>Public health and education spending as a share of GDP measures fiscal effort, not universality, not\n          quality, and not usage by the middle class. Two countries with identical spending shares can differ in\n          whether public hospitals serve the well-off or only the poor. The proxy bias is conservative: measurement\n          error in the gate variable attenuates the interaction and biases against confirmation.</p>\n          <h3><span class=\"limno\">3.</span>Identification of the gate</h3>\n          <p>The welfare measure is pre-determined relative to erosion onset, but it is not randomly assigned; the\n          first democratic decade is itself a period of democratic politics, and governments that consolidated well\n          also maintained services. The balancing regressions, legacy-instrument 2SLS, within-Eastern-Europe\n          estimate, placebo moderator and early-erosion exclusion each address a specific version of this threat, but\n          none eliminates a third factor, state capacity, geography or geopolitical alignment, that drives both\n          welfare maintenance and democratic resilience. EU accession was itself a welfare-building force, so the\n          gate and the accession channel are partially entangled by construction.</p>\n          <h3><span class=\"limno\">4.</span>Measurement of the outcome and the treatment</h3>\n          <p>The Liberal Democracy Index is expert-coded, and its inter-temporal comparability is contested. Gini\n          comparability is limited by differing underlying surveys and income concepts; PIP and WID harmonization\n          does not remove the issue. The threat to the sequencing tests is asymmetric: a misdated erosion onset could\n          manufacture the confirmation pattern for H2. The three-year sustained-decline coding rule, alternative\n          onset codings, and the requirement that the sequencing pattern differ across welfare arms address it, and a\n          pure measurement artifact would not produce that difference.</p>\n          <h3><span class=\"limno\">5.</span>The placebo subsample problem</h3>\n          <p>The sharpest contrast, H5, requires a full-sample placebo. The OECD SOCX measure exists only for OECD\n          members, so it runs as a secondary subsample with its coverage limitation quantified. If the ILO or IMF\n          full-sample transfer series proves unavailable on OWID for a substantial share of the roster, that finding\n          is itself a registered limitation, and the paper would say so.</p>\n        </section>\n\n      </main>\n\n      <footer>\n        <p class=\"cite\"><span class=\"title\">The Welfare Gate: Pre-Fisc Inequality, Universal Public Services, and\n        Democratic Resilience in Post-1990 Democratizers.</span> A pre-registered research design. Protocol, country\n        roster, coverage matrix, minimum-detectable-effect analysis and code are deposited in a timestamped OSF\n        registry before estimation; the registration ID and deposit date are fixed at the moment of deposit.</p>\n        <p class=\"cite\">No model has been estimated as of this version. A companion paper will report estimates\n        against the criteria fixed in Section 6 of the paper.</p>\n        <div class=\"f-links\">\n          <a href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-77624d-the-welfare-gate-pre-fisc-inequality@main/paper.pdf\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Paper (PDF)</a>\n          <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-77624d-the-welfare-gate-pre-fisc-inequality\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Code repository</a>\n        </div>\n        <p class=\"status\">All data are public Our World in Data (OWID) panels, with one disclosed non-OWID input,\n        the Boix&ndash;Miller&ndash;Rosato cross-check for transition dating. Every series is cited with its OWID\n        grapher path in the paper's coverage matrix, so the panel is reproducible without proprietary data.</p>\n      </footer>\n\n    </div>\n  </div>\n</div>\n\n<script>\n(function () {\n  \"use strict\";\n  var ids = [\"overview\", \"contributions\", \"method\", \"results\", \"limitations\"];\n  var links = Array.prototype.slice.call(document.querySelectorAll('#section-nav a'));\n  var sections = ids.map(function (id) { return document.getElementById(id); });\n\n  function setActive(id) {\n    links.forEach(function (a) {\n      if (a.getAttribute(\"href\") === \"#\" + id) {\n        a.setAttribute(\"aria-current\", \"true\");\n        a.classList.add(\"is-active\");\n      } else {\n        a.removeAttribute(\"aria-current\");\n        a.classList.remove(\"is-active\");\n      }\n    });\n  }\n\n  function currentFromScroll() {\n    var probe = window.innerHeight * 0.38;\n    var active = ids[0];\n    sections.forEach(function (sec, i) {\n      if (sec && sec.getBoundingClientRect().top <= probe) { active = ids[i]; }\n      });\n    }, { rootMargin: \"-35% 0px -58% 0px\", threshold: 0 });\n    sections.forEach(function (sec) { if (sec) { io.observe(sec); } });\n  } else {\n    window.addEventListener(\"scroll\", currentFromScroll, { passive: true });\n    currentFromScroll();\n  }\n})();\n</script>\n</body>\n</html>", "new_content": "<!DOCTYPE html>\n<html lang=\"en\">\n<head>\n<meta charset=\"utf-8\">\n<meta name=\"viewport\" content=\"width=device-width, initial-scale=1\">\n<meta name=\"description\" content=\"A pre-registered research design testing whether market-inequality surges erode post-1990 democratizers only where universal public health and education services are thin.\">\n<title>The Welfare Gate: Pre-Fisc Inequality, Universal Public Services, and Democratic Resilience in Post-1990 Democratizers</title>\n<style>\n  :root {\n    --paper: #fbfaf6;\n    --raise: #ffffff;\n    --ink: #232220;\n    --ink-soft: #5d5a52;\n    --ink-mid: #3a3833;\n    --hairline: #e5e1d5;\n    --block: #f3f0e7;\n    --accent: #17604c;\n    --accent-deep: #11483a;\n    --sans: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, \"Segoe UI\", Roboto, \"Helvetica Neue\", Arial, \"Noto Sans\", sans-serif;\n    --serif: Georgia, \"Times New Roman\", Cambria, \"Noto Serif\", serif;\n  }\n  * { box-sizing: border-box;
